S002.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
S002.description: Often has difficulty sustaining attention in tasks or play activities.
examples: Focuses at first during class or meetings but soon becomes distracted or spaces out.
Re-reads the same paragraph in a book multiple times but the content does not register.
Loses focus while watching movies or TV and misses the plot.
Unable to maintain attention until the end of a long meeting or lecture, often drifting off or becoming drowsy.

S008.name: Distractibility
S008.description: Often easily distracted by extraneous stimuli (for older adolescents and adults, may include unrelated thoughts).
examples: Easily distracted and stops working due to small noises or movements nearby.
Cannot concentrate because eyes keep wandering to the scenery outside the window or people passing by.
Starts daydreaming or gets sidetracked by sudden thoughts while working or studying.
Loses focus and listens in when hearing side conversations or TV sounds.

S009.name: Daily_Activities_Forgetfulness
S009.description: Often forgetful in daily activities (e.g., doing chores, running errands; for older adolescents and adults, returning calls, paying bills, keeping appointments).
examples: Forgets appointment times or meeting schedules, arriving late or missing them entirely.
Forgets to reply to received calls or messages for days.
Frequently incurs late fees because of missing deadlines for utility bills or credit card payments.
Forgets to take medication or leaves necessary items at home when going out.

S010.name: Fidgeting
S010.description: Often fidgets with or taps hands or feet or squirms in seat.
examples: Constantly shaking legs or twisting and squirming body while seated.
Spinning a pen or fiddling with nearby objects, unable to keep hands still.
Continually changing posture and feeling uncomfortable while sitting.
Constantly moving, such as tapping the desk with fingers or tapping feet on the floor.

S011.name: Leaving_Seat
S011.description: Often leaves seat in situations when remaining seated is expected.
examples: Frequently leaves seat or wanders around during class or meetings using excuses.
Unable to sit still during meals and keeps getting up.
Leaves seat in the middle of a movie or performance to go to the restroom or go outside.
Continually leaves seat and wanders around in the office where one is expected to sit and work.

S012.name: Feeling_Restless
S012.description: Often runs about or climbs in situations where it is inappropriate. (Note: In adolescents or adults, may be limited to feeling restless.)
examples: Feels uncomfortable and restless as if something is squirming inside when sitting still.
Feels internally anxious and stifled in situations requiring prolonged sitting.
A sense of urgency and anxiety that one must keep moving or doing something.
Feels unable to endure staying still and must constantly be doing something.

S013.name: Quiet_Activity_Difficulty
S013.description: Often unable to play or engage in leisure activities quietly.
examples: Unable to engage in calm activities for long, such as reading quietly or drawing.
Cannot play quietly, often shouting or making loud noises during games or play.
Unable to stay quiet in quiet places like libraries or movie theaters, making noise.
Cannot endure and avoids quiet and calm activities like meditation or yoga.

S015.name: Excessive_Talking
examples: Talks incessantly and cannot tolerate silence, continuing to chatter.
Continues to talk even when others are bored or try to cut the conversation short.
Talks too much inappropriately for the situation, making people around them uncomfortable.
Monopolizes the conversation and gives almost no chance for others to speak.

S018.name: Interrupting_Intruding
S018.description: Often interrupts or intrudes on others (e.g., butts into conversations, games, or activities).
examples: Butts into conversations of others where they have not been invited.
Joins in on others' work or games without permission or interferes.
Touches or uses other people's belongings or work without permission.
Keeps talking to and disturbing others when they are focusing on work or studying.

symptom.disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation, is characterized by developmentally inappropriate levels of motor activity, impulsivity, and difficulty inhibiting behavior, with comparatively fewer or less prominent inattentive features. In adults, the presentation often shifts from overt running and climbing to inner restlessness, difficulty remaining seated, and acting without forethought in work and social contexts. Symptoms must be present for at least six months, cause clinically significant impairment in multiple settings, and are typically rooted in childhood, even if they become more impairing or noticeable in adulthood due to increased role demands. It is distinguished from anxiety, mood, and personality disorders by its early onset, pervasive pattern of disinhibition and activity level, and the absence of episodic mood changes as the primary driver of difficulties.

patient.personality: Edileusa is an energetic, conscientious supervisor who thrives on social interaction, dancing, and self-improvement while juggling work responsibilities with an active nightlife.
patient.stressor: Around fourteen months ago, Edileusa was promoted from caregiver to care-team supervisor, taking on responsibility for coordinating multiple aides’ schedules, handling urgent family calls, and documenting care plans for a growing roster of elderly clients. The promotion dramatically increased the amount of information she had to juggle at once—phone calls, messaging apps, electronic records, and in-person conversations—while she continued to stay up late watching films and going to dance classes, leaving her mentally taxed. Over the ensuing year, she noticed that her mind constantly drifted to other tasks or outside distractions during important planning sessions and documentation work, causing mix-ups in schedules, missed follow-ups, and tension with both staff and families who depended on her accuracy. After a near-miss where a client’s medication visit was almost skipped due to her losing track of details during a hectic shift, her supervisor expressed concern and suggested she get an evaluation, prompting her to seek psychiatric help because she felt unable to keep her attention where it needed to be despite her strong motivation to do well.
patient.chief_complaint: “I get distracted so easily at work that I lose track of what I’m doing, even when it’s important.”

S002.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
S002.description: Often has difficulty sustaining attention in tasks or play activities.
S002.manifestation: When I'm in the office trying to finish a care plan or double-check the aides’ schedules, I start out focused, but within a few minutes my mind just slips away to random things—like what song we danced to last night or what I want to cook later—and I end up rereading the same line over and over without it sticking.

S008.name: Distractibility
S008.description: Often easily distracted by extraneous stimuli (for older adolescents and adults, may include unrelated thoughts).
S008.manifestation: I can be on an important call with a client’s daughter, and the second someone walks by the doorway, a phone pings, or I catch a bit of music from someone’s radio, my attention jumps there and I miss half of what the person on the phone is saying.

S009.name: Daily_Activities_Forgetfulness
S009.description: Often forgetful in daily activities (e.g., doing chores, running errands; for older adolescents and adults, returning calls, paying bills, keeping appointments).
S009.manifestation: I keep forgetting really basic stuff, like calling families back when I said I would, bringing the right forms to a home visit, or even paying my phone bill on time, and I only remember when someone chases me or I get a late notice.

S010.name: Fidgeting
S010.description: Often fidgets with or taps hands or feet or squirms in seat.
S010.manifestation: I’m always bouncing my leg, clicking my pen, twisting my hair, or drumming my fingers on the desk, and even in meetings I’ll catch myself shifting around and tapping so much that people glance at me because I just can’t keep still.

S011.name: Leaving_Seat
S011.description: Often leaves seat in situations when remaining seated is expected.
S011.manifestation: During team meetings or trainings, I can’t stay in my chair—I keep popping up to refill my water, pretend I need the bathroom, or go check something “urgent” in the hallway because sitting there the whole time feels unbearable.

S012.name: Feeling_Restless
S012.description: Often runs about or climbs in situations where it is inappropriate. (Note: In adolescents or adults, may be limited to feeling restless.)
S012.manifestation: It feels like I have a motor inside me that never shuts off—when I’m supposed to be sitting quietly doing documentation or even just watching a movie with friends, I get this crawling, trapped feeling in my body and I have to get up, pace, or start doing something else.

S013.name: Quiet_Activity_Difficulty
S013.description: Often unable to play or engage in leisure activities quietly.
S013.manifestation: Even in my so-called relaxing time, like watching a film at home or doing an online dance class, I’m talking over the movie, rewinding, checking my phone, singing along too loud, or jumping up to try moves in the middle of the room because I can’t just sit and do it calmly.

S015.name: Excessive_Talking
S015.manifestation: Once I start talking, especially at work or when we go out after my shift, I just keep going—explaining every little detail of my day, cutting in with stories, filling every silence—and I only realize I’ve been dominating the conversation when I see people zoning out.

S018.name: Interrupting_Intruding
S018.description: Often interrupts or intrudes on others (e.g., butts into conversations, games, or activities).
S018.manifestation: I constantly cut people off in mid-sentence during handovers or family meetings, finishing their thoughts or jumping in with my ideas, and I’ll lean over aides while they’re charting to point things out or grab their mouse without asking, then later feel bad when I see they’re annoyed.
